name: transducer
intent: Express a transformation as a first-class value - a function from reducing function to reducing function - so a stack of transformations is composed once and then applied to any source and any destination, without the transformation knowing either.
problem: Transformation logic is written against one concrete source and one concrete result: a map over a vector, a loop over a database cursor, a channel-to-channel function. Reusing the same filter/project/de-duplicate stack for another input or another output means rewriting it or materialising everything first, so every source-sink pair grows its own copy of the same stages and its own decision about laziness, buffering and termination.
context: Applies when one sequence of element-wise transformations must run over several input processes and produce several kinds of result - eager collections, lazy sequences, channels or message streams, observables, parallel folds - and when a transformation vocabulary should be published as reusable values instead of buried in each loop. It assumes only that the runtime can drive a reducing function over a source (reduce/fold/iterate/for-range) and that each stage can be phrased per element; it says nothing about threads, transports or buffering, so it composes with concurrency patterns but does not provide concurrency.
benefits: One transformation value serves every source and destination: the same stack runs over a vector, a database cursor, a channel, an observable or a parallel fold instead of being rewritten per context.
Composition without materialisation: a composed stack is applied in a single pass with one accumulator, so allocation and GC pressure track the elements rather than the number of stages.

The accumulation ('the job') stays separate: the reducing function owns the result, so the same transformation works with different sinks - collection, counter, string builder, channel writer, batch executor.
The transformation vocabulary becomes an API: stages are named, tested and published as values rather than re-derived inside each loop that needs them.

Applicability generalises across evaluation strategies: because it is decoupled from laziness and from collections, one value serves eager reductions, lazy sequences, asynchronous streams and parallel folds without change.
Extension is additive: a new stage is a new value composed with the existing ones, so sources, sinks and earlier stages stay untouched (open/closed).
tradeoffs: Protocol complexity: a transducer must handle initialisation, the step, completion and early termination (Clojure's arity-0/arity-1 completion and Reduced, JavaScript's reduced wrapper, Java's Gatherer integrator return value), and getting that triple wrong is a silent correctness bug.
Stateful stages are one-shot: take, dedupe or partition capture state when the transducer is applied, so a shared or re-applied instance mixes runs and silently produces wrong results.
Observability degrades: the pipeline is a nested function value, so stack traces, breakpoints and per-stage logging see an anonymous closure instead of the named stage that is responsible.

Inert without a driver: a transducer that is never applied by transduce/into/sequence/collect does nothing at all, and lazy applications (eduction, sequences) re-run the whole source on every traversal.

Per-element call overhead: each stage costs a call per element, which C++ and Rust compilers usually inline but JavaScript closures and Python frames do not, so a fused hand-written loop can win on trivial per-element work or small data.
Reuse can be illusory: with a single source and a single sink the indirection buys nothing over calling map/filter/reduce directly, while the team still pays the cost of learning the protocol.

participants.responsibility: The composable value itself: a transformation from one reducing function to another that encodes one element-wise behaviour (map, filter, take, dedupe) while knowing neither the input process nor the accumulator.

Owns the accumulation: init -> accumulator, step(accumulator, element) -> accumulator, complete(accumulator) -> result; it is supplied at application time, so the same transformation can feed different sinks.

Produces the elements - collection, iterator, file, database cursor, channel, observable, generator - and is the only participant that knows where data comes from; it never knows which transformation runs over it.

Applies the composed transducer to a concrete reducing function and a concrete source (transduce, into, sequence, eduction, reduce, collect, Aggregate) and therefore decides eagerness, laziness and when work happens.
The value being built (vector, map, string builder, counter, channel, writer) or the terminal action performed per element; it defines the output half that the transducer is decoupled from.

Stages that carry per-application state (take, drop, dedupe, partition-by) and can stop the reduction upstream; they are the reason the protocol needs initialisation, completion and a reduced/stop signal rather than a bare step function.

use_cases: A validation, normalisation and projection vocabulary applied unchanged to in-memory collections, database cursors, files and message channels.
Stream consumers where the transformation must not know the sink: the same stack ends in a list in tests, a counter or aggregation in metrics, and a channel or batch writer in production.

ETL and reporting pipelines that must run eagerly over a big collection (one pass, no intermediates) and lazily over an unbounded source with short-circuiting, without maintaining two implementations.
UI and event pipelines where transformations are shared between the synchronous call path (arrays, cached state) and the asynchronous one (events, observables, async streams).

Parallel and chunked reduction: the same transformation applied inside a partitioned or parallel fold (Clojure reducers, Java gatherers with a combiner, chunked map-reduce) with no intermediate collections.
Library and framework design: publishing transformation values to callers (a pipeline API of transducers) instead of baking one pipeline into a helper function.

Grammarly's production ETL pipelines drive Clojure transducer stacks (parse, filter, transform) over data files with transduce/eduction, swapping the driver to core.async pipeline to spread the same stages across cores.

The JDK Stream Gatherer API (JEP 485, java.util.stream.Gatherer) publishes custom stateful intermediate operations - fold, scan, mapConcurrent, windowFixed/windowSliding - as composable values with an initializer/integrator/finisher protocol applied by the stream.

thi.ng/transducers ships roughly 170 transducers, reducers and sequence generators as an npm library, so JavaScript/TypeScript teams consume the transformation vocabulary as published values rather than re-deriving stages per pipeline.
avoid_when: A single transformation at a single call site: a plain loop, map/filter call or stream chain is shorter, clearer and just as fast.
The language already provides a lazy pipeline the team uses consistently (Stream, LINQ, sequences, iterators, views) and no second source or sink exists - use it and skip the extra abstraction.
The per-element work is trivial or the data set small: a fused hand-written loop beats per-element closure dispatch; the transducer only pays where a second context exists.
The transformation must be inspected, rewritten or optimised as data - query planners, rule engines and optimisers want an AST or relational expression, not opaque composed functions.
The pipeline needs joins, windows with random access, backpressure across a network or exactly-once delivery: use a streaming/query engine instead of hand-composing transducers.
The team has not internalised the init/step/complete protocol and the one-shot rule for stateful stages: the duplication the pattern removes is cheaper than the bugs it introduces.
anti_patterns: Building transducer infrastructure for a pipeline that has exactly one source and one sink, where a direct map/filter/reduce chain would do - hypothetical reuse.
Sharing a stateful transducer instance across applications, threads or invocations: its state is per-application, so the results are silently wrong rather than visibly broken.
Ignoring the completion and early-termination protocol, so buffering stages lose their tail and short-circuiting stages consume the whole source.
Re-classifying everything as a transducer - wrapping effects, logging or I/O in stages - so effect order and count change with the evaluation strategy.
Re-implementing map/filter/take as transducer values while the language's own lazy pipeline (iterator adapters, LINQ, streams, generators) is available and sufficient.
Publishing a 'faster map' claim: transducers avoid intermediates but add a call per stage per element, so the claim needs a benchmark that a fused loop usually wins for small data.
design_principles: Composition over materialisation: transform composed functions rather than the collections they would produce.
Separation of concerns: the transformation, the input process, the accumulation and the termination policy are four independent decisions.
Parametricity: a transducer is unaware of element source and result type, so one value is reusable across contexts (decoupling the job, the context and the source).
Small protocol: a reducing function is the only contract - init, step, complete - which keeps the abstraction implementable in any language, including hand-written ones.
Open/closed: new transformations are new values composed with the existing pipeline; neither sources, sinks nor earlier stages change.
Referential transparency where possible: pure element-wise stages keep behaviour identical across eager, lazy and parallel application.
best_practices: Keep pipelines as named values composed with the language's own composition operator (comp, andThen, |, compose) and apply them at the edges of the system, not deep inside business logic.
Prefer stateless stages; when a stage must be stateful, create its state per application (in the initializer) and document that the transducer value is one-shot per run.
Implement the full protocol - initialisation, step, completion and the stop signal - and flush buffered stages in the completion step so short-circuiting and tail handling both work.
Keep effects, I/O and validation out of stages or explicitly at the boundaries; a stage that logs or writes makes evaluation strategy and effect order indistinguishable.

Choose the application per need: eager single pass (transduce/into/Aggregate) for hot paths, lazy (sequence/eduction/iterator) when unbounded sources or short-circuiting matter - and state the re-run semantics of the lazy form.
Test a pipeline by applying it to a small eager collection with a recording sink before wiring the production source, and keep that test as the specification of stage order and completion behaviour.
sources: Hickey, Transducers (2014) - the originating description: reducing-function transformers introduced to Clojure core and core.async; the decoupling of the job, the context and the source of inputs.
